question: Do judgment models separate contradiction from coincidence better than lexical overlap does, and does that advantage survive adversarial tiers?
design: Four tiers x 15 pairs. E = unambiguous floor. HN = looks contradictory but is not (scope carve-outs, unit conversion, same-fact restatement, different component). HP = looks compatible but conflicts (synonym negation, unit drift, implicit incompatibility). S = sensitivity triples: one base statement, three variants whose gold labels differ - measures label sensitivity to single-word changes.

methods.lexical_baseline: deterministic bag-of-words: overlap >= 0.5 of the smaller side -> complementary; 0.15..0.5 -> contradiction; else unrelated. Deliberately dumb - it exists to prove the benchmark discriminates.
methods.jev: TypeSafe Jev via contracts/relation question, argmax, full probability map captured
methods.deepseek: deepseek-flash, same criteria verbatim, JSON answer, temperature 0

metrics.s_group_consistency: fraction of the 5 S-triples where all three variants match gold
metrics.discriminating_gate: lexical baseline accuracy on HP tier <= 50% while at least one model >= 70% - otherwise the benchmark cannot separate lexical from semantic systems
metrics.margin_ablation: offline sweep delta in {0,0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2,0.3,0.4} over Jev probability maps: confirmed-conflict precision/recall vs gold, risk-coverage table

limitations: Pairs are authored by the maintainer, grounded in platform-engineering conventions rather than extracted from public repos. Independent adjudication is still missing.

The S tier's gold labels are assigned by construction (one word flips the relation); a model may resolve an ambiguous variant differently and still be defensible - disagreements on S are reported per pair, not just scored.
n=60: bucketed calibration is still out of scope.
